sections.h2: Where is Monmouth County, NJ, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Monmouth County occupies the central coast of New Jersey, bordered by Middlesex and Mercer Counties to the west, Ocean County to the south, the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Raritan Bay to the north. Wikipedia reports 661.40 square miles in total, but only 468.18 are land, because 29.2% of the county's area is water.

Freehold Borough is the county seat, although many county offices also sit in neighboring Freehold Township. Middletown Township is the most populous municipality, with 67,106 residents in 2020, and Howell Township is the largest by area at 61.21 square miles. The county holds fifty-three municipalities, according to the ranking listed for Middletown on Wikipedia.

The land is mostly low and flat. Hills rise around Holmdel, where Crawford Hill is the county's highest point at roughly 380 to 391 feet, and in the Locust section of Middletown and the boroughs of Highlands and Atlantic Highlands. The shore towns, from Long Branch and Asbury Park down to Spring Lake, set the market for oceanfront homes, while western towns such as Freehold, Marlboro and Colts Neck are inland and more rural.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Monmouth County?
sections.html:
Municipal offices send the bills. Each of the county's towns has its own assessor and tax collector, and the Monmouth County Board of Taxation oversees assessments and hears appeals. The board's assessment information page gives its address as the Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728, and its phone number as (732) 431-7404.

The board has five members appointed by the governor, and it hears disputes about assessments, with the municipality represented by its attorney. All of its meetings are public. The county also offers a property tax estimator through its record search, and the Township of Middletown's page points owners to that tool for projecting a bill.

For a payoff before closing, call the collector for the town where the house stands. Your title company will ask that town's tax office for the figure.

sections.h2: What makes the Monmouth County appeal calendar different?
sections.html:
Monmouth follows an alternate assessment calendar, and the tax appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. The New Jersey Division of Taxation names Monmouth, Burlington and Gloucester as the three counties on that calendar in its appeal guide. Hearings are generally held after the January 15 deadline, and the board generally denies adjournments.

The county's appeal page adds these details:

  • An assessment is presumed correct, so the owner must prove it is excessive or discriminatory.
  • Evidence should relate to the October 1 assessment date, and at least three comparable sales go to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board a week before the hearing if they were not filed with the petition.
  • All taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter must be paid to the collector.
  • Owners of income-producing property must supply an income statement on the board's forms.
  • A skipped hearing leads to dismissal for lack of prosecution.

A dissatisfied owner has 45 days from the mailing of the judgment to appeal to the Tax Court of New Jersey. If the assessment is over $1,000,000, the owner can file directly with the Tax Court by April 1. The board also explains the Chapter 123 test: when the ratio of assessment to true value exceeds the average ratio by more than 15%, the assessment is reduced to the common level.

sections.h2: How does annual reassessment work in Monmouth County?
sections.html:
Monmouth took part in an Assessment Demonstration Program created by P.L. 2013, c. 15, which moved the county toward more frequent reassessment. Middletown's assessment page cites a Monmouth University study that found both vertical and horizontal inequity in residential assessments dropped after the program began, and notes that the county's assessors association and tax board received a 2019 Distinguished Jurisdiction Award from the International Association of Assessing Officers.

For owners, that history has a practical effect. Values are updated more often, so a change in the assessment notice reflects recent sales instead of waiting for a one-time revaluation. Middletown reported that its aggregate preliminary net value for tax year 2026 was 7.94% above 2025 and that the rate was expected to fall as a result. An owner can look up property record cards, sales data and prior postcards in the county's online record search before deciding to appeal.

sections.h2: How has the shore shaped Monmouth County property values?
sections.html:
Hurricane Sandy in 2012 hit the northern Jersey Shore hard, and Wikipedia reports that whole neighborhoods in Monmouth County were demolished and rebuilt, some at a higher price level than before. The page ties that rebuilding to rising values in many shore communities and to purchases by buyers seeking second homes near New York.

The county's economy reaches beyond the beach. The Bell Labs Holmdel complex became a business incubator in 2016, Freehold Raceway Mall is a super-regional shopping center, and Pier Village in Long Branch anchors the oceanfront. The county's gross domestic product was $34.2 billion in 2021. For a seller, a location on the water or near a train line sets much of the price, and the assessor's record for your lot sets the tax.

sections.h2: What relief programs can Monmouth County owners use?
sections.html:
The state offers relief that applies in every county. The Division of Taxation's relief page says the fiscal year 2027 budget funds the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ programs, and that the 2025 application deadline was November 2, 2026. Local assessors handle the senior, disabled and veteran deductions on the municipal side. In Middletown, for example, the assessor's office assists with senior and veteran relief and with a review of a property record card.

A sale during the year may change eligibility, so ask the state program office how a mid-year move affects a claim before you close.

faqs.q: What is the Monmouth County property tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: January 15. Monmouth uses an alternate assessment calendar, and the statewide April 1 date does not apply to most owners. An assessment over $1,000,000 can go directly to the Tax Court by April 1.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Monmouth County Board of Taxation?
faqs.a: Call (732) 431-7404 or write to the County Board of Taxation, Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728. The board can send the forms needed to file an assessment appeal.

faqs.q: What if I disagree with the Monmouth County Tax Board's decision?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date the judgment was mailed to file a further appeal with the Tax Court of New Jersey. Missing a hearing leads to dismissal for lack of prosecution, which can block that next step.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Monmouth County property tax bill itself?
faqs.a: No. Taxes come from local budgets and cannot be appealed. You can challenge only the assessment, and you must pay all taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter while the appeal is pending.

faqs.q: How many comparable sales do I need for a Monmouth County appeal?
faqs.a: Submit at least three comparable sales. The board wants them delivered to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board at least a week before the hearing if they were not attached to the petition.
